title: Joseph's dream (Matthew 1:18–25)
hookLine: a quiet carpenter plans to step away gently, then an angel says do not be afraid
carry: the one who says nothing and stays
tomorrow: where do you put a newborn when the guest room is full?

cards: Big news lands in the group chat, and one person goes quiet. Hurt? Shock?
Respect? Everyone reads the silence differently. Joseph gets the biggest news of his life: Mary, promised to him, is with child, and the child isn't his.
Search all four Gospels for anything Joseph says. There's nothing. Not one line.
So Catholic readers have argued for centuries about what his silence meant.

teach.b: Here's what Matthew does tell us, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately."
The law of his day gave him harsher options. A just man, someone who keeps God's law, chooses the gentlest. Now the two readings.
The first goes back to John Chrysostom, an early bishop and preacher: Joseph thought the worst, and chose mercy anyway, sparing her shame even while he was hurt.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: STEPPING BACK IN AWE.
teach.b: The second runs through Bernard of Clairvaux, a medieval monk: Joseph sensed the child was holy and wanted to step back out of awe, the way Peter would later ask Jesus to depart from him, a sinful man.

Then the angel comes in a dream: "Joseph, son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, for that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Ghost." Fear not. Afraid of disgrace, say the first readers.
Afraid of holiness, say the second. Both readings live in Catholic writing, and the Church hasn't chosen between them.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.
teach.b: What nobody argues about is what came next: he woke, took Mary home, and at another dream carried his family into Egypt.
Catholics honor him as patron of the whole Church, a title Pius the Ninth gave him in 1870, with feasts on March 19 and May 1. Silent, faithful, and there.

how: Catholics honor Saint Joseph on March 19 and as Joseph the Worker on May 1, ask his prayers for families, workers and the dying, and Catholic custom dedicates Wednesdays and the month of March to him.

games.q: who reads it how — tap the pairs.

s: Joseph has a few lines in the Gospels
not one word, in any of the four Gospels.
the Gospels say Joseph was an old man
they never give his age. the elderly Joseph comes from later writings, like the Protoevangelium of James, and art.
before the dream, Joseph had already chosen to spare Mary public shame
"not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately."

games.q: you've always heard that Joseph thought Mary had been unfaithful. state the other view, Bernard's, at its strongest.
o: Joseph tells the angel he never doubted Mary for a moment.
Matthew names the Holy Ghost before Joseph decides; a just man might step back from something holy.
Joseph feared the neighbors, and "fear not" means don't fear them.
games.why: Bernard's best case: the text names the Holy Ghost first, and fear can be awe, like Peter's. Joseph never speaks, so the first can't be it. the Church holds both readings.

practice: Joseph's whole part is action without a speech, so this one is practical.

Before the sit ends, do one quiet thing for someone without being asked: rinse a cup that isn't yours, plug in a phone that's dying, set out something they'll need tomorrow. Don't mention it to anyone.

wordCard.voice: Joseph's dream. A just man, a quiet plan, an angel saying fear not, and a husband who woke up and stayed.

orig.note: Greek: just, righteous. Matthew's word for Joseph, whose righteousness chose mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who says nothing and stays. Two readings of his silence, and one thing everyone agrees on. That's day twenty-four.
